source.title: Belief/Evidence Graphic
allOriginalH2Texts: Describe the content of this graphic.
Can individual A rationally say at the end of the period, ‘I knew it all along’ if they maintained their high degree of belief without mapping it to the relevant evidence as it fluctuated?
Was individual C rational to wait until the evidence reached a particular threshold to flip from disbelief to belief?
Provide three scenarios in which the cost of belief would be high, epistemically justifying disbelief.
In your three secnarios, what would be the actual danger of mapping one’s belief to the degree of the evidence?
But a credence is not a decision. Wouldn’t more accurate credences better inform the decisions?
All things being equal, including the credibility of the evidence, is it not better to update your priors as new confirming and disconfirming evidence arrives?
Then, based on your last response, it would have been more rational for C to have updated their credences to map to the changing balance of evidence, right?
You said the following:

However, there was no suggestion in my scenario that the evidence was anything other than reliable evidence. There is no “whim”, and therefore, C would be irrational not to constantly adjust their degree of belief as the degree of the non-whimsical evidence arrived, right?
Provide a salient reformulation of the notion that rational belief is a degree of belief that maps to the degree of the relevant evidence.
For a final confirmation, explain why individual B was or was not the most rational of the three individuals.
If the degree of B’s belief did map to the degree of the evidence, B would be most rational of the three individuals, correct?
Then it is correct to say rational belief is a degree of belief that maps to the degree of the relevant evidence. Right?
Create an 8-item quiz on the discussion above.
Provide 15 discussion questions relevant to the content above.

source.title: Pascal’s Wager
allOriginalH2Texts: Provide a comprehensive explanation of Pascal’s Wager.
According to proponents of the wager, no actual evidence for the alleged consequences of a decision for or against the alleged entity is needed for the wager to have weight. Is this correct?

If Pascal’s Wager does not depend on evidence, all that is needed to force a proponent of Pascal’s Wager to move to another alleged God is an unsubstantiated claim of a God with a better Heaven and more horrific Hell. Correct?
Since the wager depends on the emotional assessment of the consequences, Pascal’s Wager is essentially a choice to follow one’s emotions devoid of the need for evidence. Correct?
But for this wager, the logical or pragmatic choice is wholly dependent on the outcome of the emotional assessment of the consequences. Right?
Create a 7-item quiz on the discussion above.
Provide 12 discussion questions relevant to the content above.
